title: Seven practical experiments associated with openai/math
review_status: No independent peer review is documented in this repository.
ai_assistance: English reports, summaries, and publication documentation were prepared with AI assistance.

experiments.title: Shortest-superstring string storage: family 128 benchmark
experiments.report_title: Evaluate family 128 shortest-superstring storage against indexed and compressed baselines
experiments.research_question: Can overlapping byte strings share storage without sacrificing reads by original ID?
experiments.abstract: A byte-preserving shortest-common-superstring prototype is compared with plain, deduplicated, prefix-coded, block-Zstd and whole-dataset-Zstd storage on 11 datasets. It preserves IDs, order, duplicates and empty strings. Overlapping fragments benefit from shared storage, but the method is not a general compression or packing-speed improvement.
findings: For 128 overlapping binary fragments, the complete archive is 1,265 bytes, versus 8,728 for plain storage, 2,010 for block Zstd and 1,167 for whole-dataset Zstd.
64 of 66 archive attempts completed; both larger paper-construction cases reached explicit resource limits.
experiments.conclusion: Useful overlap-specific storage tradeoff; no general compressor replacement.
experiments.limitations: Packing cost, index overhead and input structure dominate practicality. Bounded oracle and round-trip tests are implementation evidence, not a proof of the full port.
experiments.review_status: No independent peer review is documented in this repository.
experiments.data_access: Synthetic/catalogue data builders are included. Stored archives and input/trace caches are omitted; new runs regenerate them.

experiments.title: Elliptic2 isolated subgraphs: degree-preserving MCMC features
experiments.report_title: Evaluate family 131 degree-preserving null features on isolated Elliptic2 subgraphs
experiments.research_question: Do family 131 degree-conditioned graph features improve suspicious-label classification?
experiments.abstract: The family 131 lazy switch kernel supplies structural residual features for a classifier on 20,000 isolated Elliptic2 subgraphs. Comparisons include ordinary NetworkX features, conventional switches, degree summaries and a directed control. The added features do not establish a convincing classification benefit on this representation.
findings: Mean test average precision (AP) is 2.288% with family 131 features, versus 2.185% for NetworkX; test positive-label prevalence is 2.275%.
The paired AP gain is +0.103 percentage points, with a conditional 95% interval of [-0.092, +0.623]. Median full-run time rises from 27.43 to 46.94 seconds.
experiments.conclusion: No convincing incremental AP benefit on isolated subgraphs.
experiments.limitations: The uncertainty is conditional on a fixed split and fitted models. Finite-budget MCMC mixing is unverified, and these features are not calibrated fraud probabilities.
experiments.review_status: No independent peer review is documented in this repository.
experiments.data_access: Raw Elliptic2 data, row-level IDs, graph samples, features and predictions are omitted. Local acquisition is required; dataset licensing is separate.

experiments.title: Elliptic2 neighboring context: graph features and MCMC ablation
experiments.report_title: Test whether one-hop Elliptic2 context changes the value of family 131 null features
experiments.research_question: Does real transaction context help, and does family 131 sampling add anything beyond it?
experiments.abstract: A separate sample of 6,000 previously unused Elliptic2 subgraphs adds split-isolated one-hop transaction context, a directed control and uncertainty estimates accounting for shared test context. Ordinary context features improve the measured result. Family 131 null features add no convincing incremental benefit.
findings: On this new sample, mean AP increases from 2.52% for core-only graphs to 6.01% with ordinary context; directed context reaches 9.51%.
Context plus family 131 achieves 6.08% AP. Its +0.07-percentage-point gain over the context baseline has a context-component 95% interval of [-1.94, +1.49].
experiments.conclusion: Context helps on this split; incremental MCMC benefit remains unestablished.
experiments.limitations: Comparisons are within the new fixed sample; they are not comparisons against the earlier isolated-study split. No temporal holdout or finite-run mixing guarantee is established.
experiments.review_status: No independent peer review is documented in this repository.
experiments.data_access: Raw transaction data, IDs, edges, graph samples, feature matrices and predictions are omitted. The guide describes local acquisition and the approximately 24.5 GB compressed context scan.

experiments.title: Metric k-median: feasibility audit and LP rounding pilot
experiments.report_title: Audit family 125 feasibility and benchmark an explicitly heuristic LP rounding pipeline
experiments.research_question: Can the published construction be instantiated cheaply, and what does a separate LP heuristic achieve?
experiments.abstract: A source audit examines the literal preparation recipe for family 125. A distinct heuristic, LP-DR16-swap, combines assignment LP, dependent rounding and local swaps in a 380-run pilot. Exact small-instance solutions and rational lower bounds help assess quality separately from solver success flags.
findings: Across ten medium/real tasks, the mean dataset-median gap to a certified lower bound is 0.136% for LP-DR16-swap versus 0.451% for FasterPAM.
Median fresh algorithm times are 906.35 ms for LP-DR16-swap and 2.32 ms for FasterPAM; the complete-process comparison is much closer.
At epsilon = 0.1, the literal sufficient preparation recipe implies Delta >= 6.08522 x 10^28.
experiments.conclusion: A costly heuristic quality check, with no per-instance dominance or evaluation of the full construction.
experiments.limitations: The full family 125 construction is not implemented. Its approximation guarantee does not transfer to LP-DR16-swap. Gaps to lower bounds are upper bounds on relative suboptimality, not necessarily exact optimality gaps.
experiments.review_status: No independent peer review is documented in this repository.
experiments.data_access: Papers, external snapshots, wheels, UCI Seeds input and some worker/cache files are omitted. Raw JSONL, tables and audit records are included; the guide distinguishes restoration from full archived-run verification.

experiments.title: OneBatchPAM versus FasterPAM: scaling and rare-client coverage
experiments.report_title: Measure OneBatchPAM scaling and rare-client failures against FasterPAM
experiments.research_question: When does client sampling save resources, and what quality is lost on rare remote groups?
experiments.abstract: This follow-up benchmarks packaged FasterPAM and OneBatchPAM in 576 isolated runs over 42 synthetic datasets with 1,000 to 10,000 clients. It measures complete-client cost and rare-group coverage separately from the sampled objective. The full family 125 approximation algorithm is outside the implementation.
findings: At N = 10,000 and k = 20, auto OneBatchPAM is 36.69x faster for distance construction plus fitting and 4.75x faster for the complete process. Peak memory is 147.9 versus 486.9 MiB.
Median full-client cost differences from the same-dataset FasterPAM baseline are +0.28% for balanced data, +183.61% for rare triplets and +93.52% for rare singletons.
The first tested size with at least 10% savings in both algorithm time and peak memory is N = 3,000.
experiments.conclusion: Substantial resource savings can come with severe rare-client failures.
experiments.limitations: These are synthetic stress cases and heuristic-to-heuristic comparisons, not gaps to a certified optimum. Larger batches improve coverage, but full coverage at a full batch retains full-matrix memory.
experiments.review_status: No independent peer review is documented in this repository.
experiments.data_access: Synthetic builders, measurements and aggregate evidence are included. Some raw worker/cache artifacts and reference downloads are omitted; follow the guide for restoration and new runs.

experiments.title: P2P broadcast topology: random regular, spectral selection and LPS graphs
experiments.report_title: Benchmark spectral topology selection for P2P broadcast and audit family 178 feasibility
experiments.research_question: Does spectral topology selection improve broadcast beyond an ordinary random regular graph?
experiments.abstract: A discrete-event flooding simulation compares rings, random regular graphs, bounded numerical spectral selection and a classical LPS construction. The pilot covers 80 constructions, 480 scenarios and 3,840 messages. It separates ordinary connectivity effects from benefits attributable to spectral selection.
findings: With 2,048 nodes, degree 4, heterogeneous latency and no failures, median time to 95% delivery falls from 33.248 seconds for a ring to 0.589 seconds for a random regular graph.
Spectral selection adds no consistent gain. LPS median paired delivery-time changes range from -2.0% to +1.7%, below the prespecified 10% improvement threshold.
experiments.conclusion: Global connectivity helps; additional spectral-selection gains are not established.
experiments.limitations: The full deterministic family 178 construction is not implemented or benchmarked. The model is finite-burst eager flooding, not a live Gossipsub deployment. Pre-failure spectral quality does not guarantee delivery after failures.
experiments.review_status: No independent peer review is documented in this repository.
experiments.data_access: Simulation code, message tables and selected verification/provenance records are published. The guide lists omitted graph and reference artifacts needed for complete archived-run checks.

experiments.title: Matrix-exponential actions: practical effect of a Crouzeix constant-2 bound
experiments.report_title: Evaluate family 325 truncation bounds and their practical effect on matrix-exponential actions
experiments.research_question: Does a tighter Crouzeix truncation bound materially reduce work for exp(A)x?
experiments.abstract: A restricted disk/Taylor prototype uses the scalar consequence of the pinned family 325 theorem to choose a polynomial degree for exp(A)x. Rational arithmetic checks the numerical-range enclosure and exact-arithmetic truncation bound. The experiment separates changing the constant from reusing polynomial preparation.
findings: Replacing 1 + sqrt(2) with 2 tightens a fixed-polynomial bound by 17.16%, but lowers degree by one in only 4 of 45 matched pairs.
Across the nonnormal case/tolerance combinations, total per-vector sparse matrix-vector products fall from 2,210 to 2,206, a 0.18% reduction.
experiments.conclusion: A useful restricted bound with little measured work reduction from the constant alone.
experiments.limitations: The certificate is conditional on the published theorem and does not certify complete float64 error. Repeated-input reuse can help with the older constant as well. The experiment is not an independent proof of the complete theorem.
experiments.review_status: No independent peer review is documented in this repository.
experiments.data_access: Measurements, case metadata and validation summaries are included. Matrix caches, output vectors and some downloaded sources are omitted; exact archived-run numerical validation needs the omitted outputs.
